name: Life Transitions & Turning Points
description: An example template for a narrative interview about how a personal network was reshaped by a major life change. The participant tells the story of a transition they nominate, while the interviewer builds the network alongside them on a single canvas. The finished network is then explored through a Narrative Interface.

items.content:
## For researchers

_Delete this screen before you field the study._

This is an **interviewer\-led narrative interview**. It is not a questionnaire a participant can work through alone. In this interview, the participant tells the story of a life change while you build their network on the Network Composer stage, and you then visualize and discuss that network on the Narrative stage.

**Plan how you will capture the discussion.** The Narrative stage collects nothing, and free\-draw annotations fade rather than being saved. You might, for example, use screen\-recording and audio\-recording software to keep a record of what is said and drawn.

### Sources

- [Herz A, Peters L, Truschkat I (2015). How to do Qualitative Structural Analysis. ](https://www.qualitative-research.net/index.php/fqs/article/view/2092)[_Forum Qualitative Sozialforschung_](https://www.qualitative-research.net/index.php/fqs/article/view/2092)[ 16(1)](https://www.qualitative-research.net/index.php/fqs/article/view/2092). — the interview procedure this template reproduces.
- [Ryan L, Mulholland J, Agoston A (2014). Talking Ties. ](https://doi.org/10.5153/sro.3404)[_Sociological Research Online_](https://doi.org/10.5153/sro.3404)[ 19(2).](https://doi.org/10.5153/sro.3404)
- [Hollstein B, Töpfer T, Pfeffer J (2020). Collecting egocentric network data with visual tools. ](https://doi.org/10.1017/nws.2020.4)[_Network Science_](https://doi.org/10.1017/nws.2020.4)[ 8(2):223–250.](https://doi.org/10.1017/nws.2020.4)

introductionPanel.title: About this interview
introductionPanel.text:
This is a **conversation**, not a questionnaire. We would like you to tell us about a time your life changed in an important way, and about the people who were part of that story.

As you talk, the interviewer will **create a network** of the people you mention on the screen in front of you. You can correct it at any point — if someone is missing, or in the wrong place, just say so.

The people you name are recorded only by the first name or nickname you choose. The interviewer will tell you before you start whether the session is being recorded, and what happens to that recording.

You can skip anything, pause, or stop at any time, and you do not have to give a reason. The researcher will answer any questions you have before you choose below.

fields.prompt: Do you consent to participate in this study?

stages.label: The change we'll be talking about

introductionPanel.title: Tell us what happened
introductionPanel.text: Think of a time in the last few years when **your life changed in an important way**. It might be something you chose, or something that happened to you.

fields.hint: An approximate month and year is fine. This becomes the reference point for the questions about 'before' and 'since'.

fields.prompt: In a few sentences, what happened?

stages.label: The people in your story
stages.interviewScript:
You should operate this interface throughout, building the map while listening to the participant's narration. Add each person when they are mentioned, using the first name or nickname the participant chooses. Automatic layout is enabled at the start to keep the map legible as it grows. Leave it on while adding people, and pause it only when you need to make a deliberate adjustment. Treat automatically produced positions as a display aid, not as evidence about closeness or importance. If position, circles, or clusters are intended to represent meaning, ask the participant what the arrangement should convey, turn off automatic layout, make the placement yourself, and confirm your interpretation. Do not impose a fixed meaning unless your study's field manual defines one. Ask open questions about how people are connected and record the configured details without interrupting the story more than necessary.

When naming slows, use the same sequence of cues with every participant. First ask whether there is anyone else they would like to add. Then prompt across contexts such as family, friends, work or study, neighborhood, community or faith groups, services and professionals, and online ties. Follow up on groups and people who know one another, while allowing uncertainty, multiple group memberships, and relationships that changed over time. Visual mapping can feel exposing, so check your entries and placements verbally, make any requested corrections yourself, avoid pressuring the participant to rank anyone precisely, and follow your study's privacy and distress procedures.

fields.label: How you know each other
fields.hint: A sentence in the participant's own words, if they give you one.

stages.label: Your network, before and since
stages.interviewScript:
You should operate this interface throughout, using the completed map as a prompt for narration rather than as an objective or complete account of the participant's network. Move through the presets selectively and ask the participant what they notice. Invite them to explain what clusters, gaps, bridges, isolated people, and changes in closeness mean in their own story. Ask about ties between people and how those relationships changed across the transition. If the participant wants to explore a different arrangement or annotate the map, make those changes yourself and confirm that they reflect what the participant intended.

Treat the map and the spoken account as complementary evidence. If they appear to diverge, explore the difference rather than correcting either one. Keep questions open, give the participant time to reflect, and follow their lead around sensitive relationships. Remind them that they may skip a question or ask you to change the map. Capture the conversation using your approved study procedure, because this stage does not save the discussion or free-draw annotations.
